questions.questionText:
Statements:
1. All Pens are Books.
2. All Books are Papers.

Conclusions:
I. Some Papers are Pens.
II. All Pens are Papers.
options: Only conclusion I follows
Only conclusion II follows
Both conclusion I and II follow
Neither conclusion I nor II follows
questions.hint: Draw Venn diagrams. A conclusion must hold in ALL valid diagrams to be considered true.
questions.explanation: Since all Pens are Books and all Books are Papers, the set of Pens is entirely contained within Papers. Hence, All Pens are Papers is true, and Some Papers are Pens is definitely true.
solutionSteps: Step 1: Venn diagram: circle of Pens is inside Books, and circle of Books is inside Papers.
Step 2: Conclusion I ("Some Papers are Pens") holds valid because Pens occupies part of Papers.
Step 3: Conclusion II ("All Pens are Papers") holds valid unconditionally.
Step 4: Both conclusions I and II follow.
questions.memoryTip: Remember: A conclusion is only definite if it cannot be disproved by any valid Venn diagram.

questions.questionText:
Statements:
1. Some Cats are Dogs.
2. All Dogs are Animals.

Conclusions:
I. Some Cats are Animals.
II. All Animals are Cats.
options: Only conclusion I follows
Only conclusion II follows
Both conclusion I and II follow
Neither conclusion I nor II follows
questions.hint: Draw Venn diagrams. A conclusion must hold in ALL valid diagrams to be considered true.
questions.explanation: The intersection between Cats and Dogs is entirely inside Animals, ensuring Some Cats are Animals. However, All Animals are Cats cannot be definitively deduced.
solutionSteps: Step 1: Some Cats are Dogs creates an overlap between Cats and Dogs.
Step 2: Since all Dogs are within Animals, the overlapping portion of Cats is also inside Animals. Thus Conclusion I follows.
Step 3: There is no guarantee that all Animals belong to Cats. Conclusion II does not follow.
